chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I said to him, 'A man swears with severe oaths that he will not buy anything for his family.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Let him buy for them, and there is nothing upon him regarding his oath.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a man swears not to buy food for his family?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Baqir (AS), the concept of 'Yamin al-Mughallazah' (severe oath) is clarified as a binding promise that requires expiation (Kaffarah) if broken, yet here it is shown to be non-obstructive to the act itself. The Imam rules that the husband may purchase provisions for his family despite the oath, indicating that the oath does not create a legal prohibition (Haram) on the transaction, but rather a personal commitment that can be fulfilled or broken with due expiation. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential distinction between an oath that prohibits an action versus one that merely binds the swearer to a specific course of conduct.

en.hubeali:
Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukeyr, from Zurara, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup>, said, ‘

I said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘The man swears with the severe oath, if he were not to buy something for his family’. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘So let him buy for them, and there is nothing upon him with regards to his oath’.
en.sarwar: 14. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from ibn Faddal from ibn Bukayr from Zurarah who has narrated the following: “I once asked abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam,
about the case of a man who takes an oath very seriously not to buy for his family. He (the Imam) said, ‘He must buy for them and he does not owe anything because of his oath.’”
